lesson: THE CALL WAS RIGHT AND THE STORY I TOLD MYSELF ABOUT IT WAS FALSE, AND THE SECOND HALF MATTERS MORE. I reasoned at 3:56 PM that 24.4 C was banked and asked whether the afternoon WOULD add >= 0.4 C, describing the trace as still rising with the peak likely 3-4 PM. It had already added +0.6 C at 2:32 PM, eighty minutes earlier, and the day was cooling while I wrote. The quantisation method survives this untouched -- the group-minus-snapshot statistic does not care where inside the window the excursion falls -- so the 82% stands on its own. But the narrative was wrong, and a narrative that rides along with a correct answer is the easiest thing in this project to promote accidentally into a finding. THE REAL RESULT IS THAT THE MECHANISM RULE IS SCORED ON A FEED THAT CANNOT SEE ITS OWN SUBJECT. It asks whether the 2/3 PM readings exceed the morning group -- a question about the continuous trace -- and is answered with the :51 lattice, the exact feed this project documents as under-reading that trace. Today snapshots said no (75.02, 75.92 vs 75.92) and the trace said yes (77.00 vs 75.92). So its 17/22 was computed from the wrong variable and should be treated as UNMEASURED, not as 77%. Worse, it cannot be repaired backwards: re-scoring needs each day's CLI peak time, and the NWS CLI archive holds about a week, so August and early September are gone for good. Forward only, which is why the time fields exist from today. Two API shapes also drifted silently and both were caught only because a number looked wrong: Kalshi candlesticks now return close_dollars strings instead of integer-cent close, so the library reader reported 'no prices' on a board trading thousands of contracts; and api.weather.gov/products/types/CLI/locations/OKX returns an EMPTY graph while 48 KOKX products sit in the type feed, so the locations route must not be trusted -- filter the type feed on issuingOffice instead. Same family as the hardcoded ladder and the hardcoded UTC offset: a shape written down once and never re-checked.

lesson: A NULL DAY LOGGED ON PURPOSE, AND IT PAID FOR ITSELF. Two straight wins for the quantisation argument invite treating it as a general edge. It is not: it only bites when the banked max lands within ~0.44 F of a .5 boundary AND that boundary is a BUCKET edge rather than an interior one. Today was mid-bucket and the market knew it, so the correct output was 'nothing to say at 99c'. A method recorded only on the days it fires will always look better than it is. THE PAYOFF WAS AN UNRELATED DEFECT IN THE PRIMARY DATA. Checking why my afternoon-group prediction missed showed the 2-8 PM group exactly equalling the morning group on 13 of 48 days, and on 11 of those the group exceeds EVERY snapshot inside its own window -- impossible from the trace. Exact equality eleven times is far more consistent with a value being carried forward than with eleven independent brief excursions that each happen to land on the morning maximum. Consequences: (1) max-of-all-same-day-groups is UNAFFECTED, since a carried value is still a true same-day max, so the 98% stands; (2) the afternoon group's standalone 83% is partly a free ride -- it is 12/12 on duplicate days and only 27/35 = 77% on the rest; (3) anything that uses the afternoon group to infer what happened IN the afternoon is contaminated, which includes the gap distribution behind the 09-16 call. That one was checked rather than assumed: excluding duplicates the distribution is 34/35 = 97% with the 0.0-to-+0.5 wall intact, and the nine shape-matched days behind the 09-16 call contain ZERO duplicates. The call survives; the statistic needed the audit anyway. The general form: I have been treating the six-hour groups as three independent measurements when on a quarter of days two of them are one measurement reported twice.

lesson: THE TWO-POINT DISTRIBUTION IS FALSIFIED. SOURCE_RELIABILITY.md called it 'the useful finding' and said in bold: 'Never negative. Never +2.' Today is +2 -- preliminary 67, final 69. Twenty-seven days of +0/+1 with zero mass elsewhere, and the twenty-eighth broke it. The doc's own honest-limits section predicted precisely this: 'A two-point distribution with zero mass elsewhere on n = 27 is exactly the kind of clean result that gets ragged with more data.' It got ragged. The mechanism is new rather than an extreme version of the old one. The eight prior misses were all +1, from a max slightly exceeding the pre-cutoff value. Here the max came at 723 PM on a warm, wet, overcast evening -- the trace sat flat at 68.0 from 17:51 to 21:51 -- so the preliminary was not marginally stale, it was measuring a different part of the day. Rain-clearing evenings with warm advection are a distinct mode and autumn will produce more of them. THE CONSEQUENCE FOR THE BUCKET ANALYSIS IS STRUCTURAL, NOT COSMETIC. The narrow-bucket certainty works by noting that prelim and prelim+1 sit inside one 2-wide bucket. But a 2-wide bucket containing both integers must START at prelim, so prelim+2 is ALWAYS outside it. Every one of the 14 genuine-2-wide days would have been broken by a +2. The 14/14 record is real but it was never the ~certainty it was described as; it is roughly 1 - P(+2), and P(+2) is no longer zero. AND MY OWN POINT ESTIMATE WAS LAZY. I called 67; it was 69. The bucket was so safe that I skipped the analysis -- and I had the exact statistic that would have warned me. On days where the 15:51 snapshot sits at or above the morning group, as today's did, P(day max exceeds the morning group by >= +0.8 C) is 14/22 = 64%. Today's excess was +1.7 C, squarely inside that distribution. I even wrote down that today was NOT the falling configuration and then did not follow the thought, because the ladder made it moot. Had the ladder been centred two degrees lower the call would have been wrong. A trivially safe bucket is a reason to state the call quickly, not a licence to stop computing the point estimate. Also: the preliminary issued at 514 PM, outside the 431-505 PM range the doc documents, so that window widens to 431-514 on n=28.

lesson: I LOST THE BUCKET CALL, AND THE METHOD BEHAVED EXACTLY AS ADVERTISED. Called 70-71 at 71%; it settled 72, inside the 72-73 bucket I had put at 28%. This is the first wrong bucket call of the run. It is NOT a methodological failure -- my own analysis assigned 28% to precisely what happened, and 28% events happen 28% of the time. The distinction matters: a calibrated method that loses is different from a broken one, and the only way to tell them apart is to have written the number down first. The market lost the same way, with 70-71 at 73c, which is no consolation and no evidence. THE QUANTISATION WALL SURVIVED ITS OWN FALSIFIER. I wrote that an excess strictly between +0.0 and +0.5 C 'would break the empirical wall, which matters more than the call'. The excess was 22.2 - 21.7 = +0.5 C EXACTLY, the modal nonzero value. The values are what settle the market, and they are the only part that has earned trust.
